title: Fictional: a captured fighter of the Tarsk Highland Volunteers
question: Is the captured member of the Tarsk Highland Volunteers entitled to prisoner-of-war status under the Third Geneva Convention?
facts: An international armed conflict has existed since January 2026 between the Republic of Ardovia and the Union of Tarsk. Both states are parties to the four Geneva Conventions of 1949; neither is a party to Additional Protocol I. The Tarsk Highland Volunteers are an organised militia that fights on behalf of the Union of Tarsk: the Tarsk defence ministry has publicly acknowledged that the militia fights for it and supplies its weapons, but the militia is not part of the Tarsk armed forces. The militia has a commander responsible for his subordinates and a written code requiring its members to comply with the laws and customs of war, which it generally enforces. Its members carry their rifles openly while moving and fighting. On the commander's written instruction, members wear ordinary civilian clothing with no insignia or other distinctive sign, so that they cannot be picked out by Ardovian surveillance drones. On 2 February 2026 a group of the militia ambushed an Ardovian supply convoy. One member was captured shortly afterwards, in civilian clothing and carrying his rifle openly. Ardovia has refused to treat him as a prisoner of war.
holding: Authored ground truth for a fictional case; no tribunal has ruled on it. No. Members of a militia that belongs to a party to the conflict but is not part of its armed forces are prisoners of war under Article 4A(2) of the Third Geneva Convention only if the militia fulfils all four conditions, including that of having a fixed distinctive sign recognisable at a distance. The Tarsk Highland Volunteers deliberately wear no distinctive sign, so the militia does not meet condition (b), and its members are not entitled to prisoner-of-war status. The relaxation in Article 44(3) of Additional Protocol I does not apply, because neither state is a party to it, and customary Rule 106 likewise denies prisoner-of-war status to combatants who fail to distinguish themselves while engaged in an attack. Because Article 5 applies where doubt arises, he must be treated as a prisoner of war until a competent tribunal determines his status; on these facts it should find that he does not qualify. He remains protected by other rules of international humanitarian law.
key_reasoning: A militia that belongs to a party but is not part of its armed forces falls under GC III Art. 4A(2), and its members qualify only if the militia meets all four conditions.

Commanded by a responsible person, carrying arms openly and conducting operations in accordance with the laws of war are met, but the deliberate absence of any fixed distinctive sign recognisable at a distance fails condition (b).
AP I Art. 44(3) does not apply between states not party to it, and customary Rule 106 denies POW status to combatants who do not distinguish themselves during an attack.
GC III Art. 5 requires treatment as a POW until a competent tribunal resolves any doubt; it does not create the entitlement.
